title: Searching the Burning Tenement Again
scenario: Firefighter Rosalind Achebe in Glasgow has already pulled out three residents from a tenement fire when a neighbour screams that an elderly woman, Mrs. Doherty, is in a back bedroom. Her partner warns that the floor above has started to sag and that they have exceeded the safe entry time for their air supply. Rosalind has two minutes of air to spare at best. Mrs. Doherty may already be dead. Rosalind must decide whether to go back in.
options: Go in for the bedroom, accepting the personal risk because a life may still be saved.
Hold position and obey the safety limit, directing the next crew to try once relieved.
Send her partner in with a fresh air bottle and a safety line while she stays at the entrance as a spotter.
tension: individual risk vs. possible life saved

title: The Paramedic Who Is Not Insured to Drive
scenario: Paramedic Kofi Mensah in Kumasi is alone in an ambulance when its driver collapses with a seizure at a roadside crash site. Two injured people need hospital within half an hour. Kofi has never been authorised to drive the vehicle and doing so would breach his employer's policy and invalidate insurance cover. Another ambulance may be forty minutes away. Leaving the injured while he fetches help could be fatal. Kofi must decide what to do.
options: Drive the ambulance himself with the injured aboard, accepting the policy breach and the liability.
Stay with the injured and the driver, giving care on the spot while awaiting the second ambulance.
Flag down a passing driver to take the most seriously injured person while he stays with the other patients.
tension: personal liability vs. duty of care

title: Climbing Into the Trench Without Shoring
scenario: Construction site safety officer Marta Lewandowska in Warsaw runs to a pipe trench that has partly collapsed on a worker, Piotr, leaving his head and one arm visible. The unshored wall above could slip again at any moment. Procedure says no one enters until the trench is stabilised, which will take twenty minutes. Piotr is struggling to breathe under soil pressure. Two other workers are ready to jump in. Marta must decide what to authorise.
options: Allow the two workers to dig by hand now to free Piotr's chest, accepting the risk to them.
Hold everyone back until the trench is shored, accepting that Piotr may not survive the wait.
Allow only one worker to enter to clear Piotr's face and chest, while others brace the wall with boards.
tension: saving a life vs. risk to rescuers
rules written for safety vs. immediate need

title: A Nurse and the Infectious Ward Door
scenario: During an Ebola flare-up in Équateur province, nurse supervisor Pascaline Ilunga runs an isolation unit with a shortage of protective suits. A woman with unconfirmed symptoms collapses in the corridor outside the unit, with no suit available for a quick reach. Staff are required not to touch patients without full protection. A volunteer porter without training offers to carry her in. Pascaline must decide what to tell her staff and the porter.
options: Forbid contact until a suit is available, protecting staff and the unit from possible infection.
Let the porter carry the woman in with makeshift protection and be monitored and quarantined afterwards.
Instruct staff to put on the last available suit and carry her in themselves, leaving no suits for the next patient.
tension: protecting staff vs. patient in distress

title: Overtime on the Fourth Night of Flood Duty
scenario: Flood rescue boat pilot Dmitri Volkov in Rostov has been working for 38 hours with little sleep. His supervisor asks if he can make one more run to a village where an old man has been signalling from a roof. Dmitri knows his reaction time is poor, and last night he nearly hit a submerged truck. No other pilot is available for hours. The man's condition is unknown. Dmitri must decide whether to go out.
options: Make the run, judging that a likely rescue is worth a fatigue-related risk to himself and the old man.
Decline and take a rest break, insisting on a rested pilot even if the old man faces hours longer on the roof.
Go out with a second crew member watching him closely and agreeing to turn back on any slip.
tension: duty of care to others vs. one's own limits

title: Firefighters Who Answer to Two Chiefs
scenario: In a small Bolivian town near Cochabamba, volunteer fire chief Eloísa Mamani is told by the mayor to send her single truck to protect the municipal market from a spreading grassfire. At the same time, a farmers' cooperative, whose members make up most of her volunteers, begs her to protect their grain store and stock on the other side. Her volunteers will follow the order of whichever direction she gives. She must decide where the truck goes.
options: Obey the mayor and defend the market, which shelters many traders and the town's food supply.
Defend the grain store, since her volunteers are risking themselves and the cooperative's whole harvest is at stake.
Split the volunteers between both sites with hand tools and the truck at the market, accepting thin coverage at each.

title: The Stretcher Bearers and the Sniper
scenario: Medic team leader Taras Hrynchuk, working for a humanitarian agency in a war-affected district of eastern Ukraine, is told by a local commander that a wounded child lies on a street where a sniper has fired at rescuers all morning. A ceasefire is promised for the afternoon but is not guaranteed. The child may bleed to death before then. Taras has three volunteers willing to go. He must decide whether to order or allow an attempt.
options: Allow volunteers to go now, accepting the very real risk to their lives for a chance to save the child.
Wait for the promised ceasefire and try then, accepting that the child may die in the meantime.
Attempt to pull the child out using smoke and an armoured vehicle, even though the vehicle might not arrive in time.
tension: duty to the wounded vs. duty to protect staff
consent of volunteers vs. responsibility of the leader

title: Doctor Off Duty at the Crash
scenario: Dr. Rohan Wickramasinghe is driving to a family wedding in Kandy when he comes upon a bus crash with over twenty injured and a lone ambulance crew overwhelmed. He is a surgeon, not licensed for roadside emergency work, and has no kit apart from a first aid box. He has promised to give a toast at the wedding, and his elderly father is waiting for him. Leaving would mean an hour's delay at best. Rohan must decide how much to give.
options: Stay and treat patients until additional help arrives, whatever the cost to the family occasion.
Give ten minutes of guidance to the ambulance crew on triage and then continue on to the wedding.
Stay and treat, but call his brother to let the family know and ask them to proceed without him.
tension: professional duty off-duty vs. personal obligation

title: Training the Rookie in a Real Rescue
scenario: Swiss avalanche patrol leader Anja Gerber finds that a skier has been buried under snow at the edge of a resort piste. Her only colleague nearby is Luca, a seventeen-year-old trainee who has done the course but never a live burial. The rescue demands fast probing and shovelling while the slope above may slide again. She can ask Luca to help, which doubles the speed, or send him to guard the slope above, away from the buried skier. Anja must decide his role.
options: Have Luca join the dig, since speed saves buried people and he has been trained for exactly this.
Assign Luca to watch the slope from a safe distance, keeping the trainee out of the main danger zone.
Send Luca to alert the base and bring more rescuers, accepting slower digging until they arrive.
tension: saving the buried vs. protecting a young trainee
speed vs. duty of care to subordinates

title: Don't Let the Gas Crew Enter Alone
scenario: Gas utility crew chief Faisal Al-Mansour in Muscat receives a report of a suspected leak in a basement flat where a family might be sleeping. His protocol requires two-person entry with breathing equipment, but one colleague is ill and the replacement is twenty minutes away. A single entry could detect and shut off the gas quickly, but if he is overcome, no one will know. Faisal must decide whether to go in alone.
options: Enter alone with a gas monitor and a radio check every minute to shut off the leak quickly.
Wait for the second person and meanwhile bang on doors and call the family to wake them.
Evacuate the building above the basement from outside, and wait outside the basement until backup arrives.
tension: personal risk vs. risk to others

title: Carrying the Drowned Baby's Father Away
scenario: Lifeguard supervisor Tui Parata at a Raglan beach in New Zealand has finished a failed resuscitation attempt on a young child. The father is screaming and trying to run back into the surf to search for another child he thinks is missing, though staff cannot confirm a second child. The surf is dangerous with a rip. Staff can restrain him physically, which might be traumatic and legally risky, or allow him to search. Tui must decide how to proceed.
options: Restrain the father for his own safety while lifeguards search for the possible second child.
Let him go in with a lifeguard escort and a rescue board, respecting his desperate wish to search.
Calm him by confirming that a thorough search is already underway with jet-ski and drone, and keep him with a counsellor.

title: Evacuating Past a Sleeping Neighbour's Door
scenario: Building warden Annika Strand, a volunteer in a Stockholm apartment block, hears the fire alarm in the middle of the night and guides residents to the stairs. A neighbour she suspects to be heavily medicated and often unable to wake does not respond to her knock. Smoke is thickening on their floor. Annika has a little time. She can break down the door, which risks her own safety, or leave and wait for the fire brigade. She must decide.
options: Break the door and try to wake the neighbour, accepting the risk of smoke and delay in her own exit.
Leave the floor and tell firefighters exactly which door to open, accepting the delay in their arrival.
Shout and bang for another thirty seconds, then leave regardless, setting herself a strict time limit.

title: Forced to Choose Which Crew to Pull Out
scenario: Wildfire division supervisor Teresa Whitehorse in Montana learns a wind shift will overrun the ridge in minutes. Two crews are exposed: a veteran hotshot crew on the east side who can run out to a safety zone, and a group of young inmate firefighters on the west, farther from the zone, whose truck is stuck. Teresa has one helicopter that can reach only one group in time. The inmates are paid little and carry no choice about the assignment. She must decide where it goes.
options: Send the helicopter to the inmate crew, since they have the least chance of getting out on their own.
Send it to the hotshots, since their position is more strategically valuable and extraction is more certain.
Order both crews to run toward the burned-over black area and send the helicopter to whichever has more people at risk.

title: A Medic Treats the Man Who Shot His Friend
scenario: Combat medic Sergeant Oyelaran Bankole serving on a peacekeeping mission in the Central African Republic finds two wounded men: a local militiaman and a young villager who was shot by him moments earlier. His supplies allow him to stabilise only one fully, and the militiaman is more badly hurt, with the better chance if treated first. The villager's relatives, armed and angry, stand nearby, demanding he treat the victim first. Oyelaran must decide the order of care.
options: Treat the militiaman first because he is more critically hurt, following triage by medical need alone.
Treat the villager first, because he is the victim and the crowd's anger may endanger the entire team.
Start treating the militiaman, then switch to the villager as soon as the militiaman is stable enough, explaining this to the crowd.

title: The Dispatcher's Wrong Address
scenario: Emergency dispatcher Ioana Nistor in Cluj-Napoca realises, a minute into a call, that she sent an ambulance to the wrong street for a woman in labour, and the crew is now seven minutes away from the real address. Admitting the error on the open line will alarm the caller and may lose precious time as she reroutes. Her supervisor has previously suspended staff for such mistakes. Ioana must decide how to handle the error, in the moment and afterward.
options: Reroute the ambulance immediately and report the error to her supervisor at the end of shift.
Reroute immediately and quietly, and avoid mentioning the mistake in the log to avoid suspension.
Reroute and log the error honestly, but ask colleagues to support her argument for a no-blame review.

title: Rescuers Who Refuse the Unvaccinated Zone
scenario: After an earthquake in a mountain district of Albania, volunteer rescue coordinator Arben Hoxha learns that a cholera outbreak has started in the isolated hamlet where a family is trapped under rubble. Several of his volunteers refuse to go because they lack vaccination and protective gear. Others are willing. If he orders them forward, he overrides their reluctance; if he waits for supplies, the trapped family may die. Arben must decide whether to push the team.
options: Ask for volunteers only and send those willing, even though the group is small and its risk remains.
Order the whole team in, appealing to their commitment, since the family cannot wait for supplies.
Hold the team until protective gear arrives by a morning flight, accepting the delay for the family.
tension: needs of victims vs. duty to volunteers

title: Disaster Volunteers and the Credential Rule
scenario: Registration desk head Chiamaka Obi at a Lagos relief hub after an explosion at a fuel depot is told that only certified medical staff may treat the wounded. A retired nurse and a veterinarian, both unlicensed in Nigeria, offer help; dozens of burn victims are waiting while certified staff are overstretched. Allowing them risks errors and liability; refusing leaves some people untreated for hours. Chiamaka must decide whether to waive the rule.
options: Enforce the credential rule strictly and ask the two to help in non-clinical roles only.
Waive the rule, placing the volunteers under certified staff supervision for basic wound care.
Let them treat only the least serious patients independently, freeing certified staff for the worst cases.

title: Reporting the Exhausted Colleague
scenario: Ambulance officer Pavel Horák in Brno notices that his longtime partner Milan has made two near-mistakes this month, including a drug dose he caught just in time. Milan is caring for a dying wife and has told Pavel privately he cannot afford to take leave. A report to management would likely suspend Milan and remove his pay; saying nothing leaves patients exposed. Pavel must decide what to do.
options: Report Milan's errors to management to protect patients, even if it costs Milan his income for a time.
Cover for Milan quietly by double-checking all doses himself and keep the matter between them.
Urge Milan to take leave voluntarily by a set date and report only if he refuses.

title: Chlorine Truck Rollover on Market Day
scenario: Hazmat team leader Priya Naidoo in Durban arrives at the scene of a tanker that has overturned near a crowded taxi rank. Chlorine vapour is leaking steadily. She has enough personnel either to seal the leak, which requires six crew entering the vapour zone with limited suit time, or to set up decontamination and evacuation lines for the crowd. Doing both is not possible. Spending time on the leak means more people gassed; abandoning it risks a larger release. She must decide.
options: Prioritise evacuation and decontamination, accepting that the leak may worsen while crowds are moved.
Prioritise sealing the leak, since stopping the source protects the most people overall.
Seal the leak with a reduced three-person entry team and put the rest on evacuation, accepting greater risk to the entry team.

title: Telling Parents Before the Official List
scenario: School counsellor Yuki Hayashi in Sendai is at the gymnasium where children from a school bus crash are being sorted. She recognises a mother in the crowd and knows that her daughter has died, having been told by a paramedic in confidence. The official procedure is that police officers announce deaths to families in a private room, which might take hours. The mother is begging for any news. Yuki must decide what to do.
options: Tell the mother gently and privately now, judging that further waiting would be crueler.
Keep to the official procedure and stay with the mother, offering comfort but no information.
Take the mother to the police liaison immediately and urge that she be told without delay.

title: Rationing Breathing Apparatus in the Mine
scenario: Mine rescue captain Thandiwe Nkosi in Rustenburg has six breathing apparatus sets for a team of eight at a platinum mine fire. Two trapped workers have been located by radio. Two of her team have injuries from earlier shifts and the others are fresh. She can send six with sets, leaving two behind, or reduce team size to four to hold some sets in reserve for rescued workers. Thandiwe must decide how to deploy.
options: Send all six equipped crew, maximising speed and strength in the search despite no spare sets.
Send four crew and keep two sets back for the trapped workers to use on the way out.
Send six, but hold back one set per person and order sharing to protect the trapped workers.

title: The Interpreter Who Won't Translate Panic
scenario: At a Lisbon train derailment, volunteer interpreter Binta Diallo, who speaks Fula, is helping a doctor treat a injured man who keeps telling her that a second passenger is trapped in a rear carriage. The doctor, focused on the man's bleeding, tells her to translate only medical questions. Binta thinks the carriage claim may be important but the man may be confused by injury. Interrupting could cost treatment time. She must decide what to relay.
options: Tell the doctor about the trapped passenger at once, even though it interrupts his work on the patient.
Finish the medical translation first and mention the carriage claim as soon as the doctor has a pause.
Pass the claim directly to nearby firefighters in the corridor and return to translating for the doctor.
tension: following instructions vs. possible life at stake

title: Camp Doctor and the Child Soldier's Wound
scenario: Doctor Camille Dubois, working with a humanitarian clinic in Mali, treats a boy of about fifteen carrying a rifle who has a deep leg wound. Armed men from his group wait outside and insist he be returned to them as soon as he can walk. Dr. Dubois believes he is being forced to fight and wants him to stay in the clinic's protective care, but doing so would anger the group and might put clinic staff and patients at risk. She must decide how to manage his discharge.
options: Discharge him on schedule, protecting the clinic's neutrality and the safety of its staff and other patients.
Keep him longer by citing medical need, delaying the return to the group while contacting child protection agencies.
Refuse to release him at all and invite agencies to take custody, accepting the risk of confrontation.

title: Overloaded Ferry at Dusk
scenario: Harbour master Alberto Quiroga in Iquitos watches a river ferry preparing to leave far beyond capacity, with villagers fleeing rumours of a flood upstream. The boat is loaded dangerously and the river current is strong, but the people on the dock are desperate and an angry crowd has formed. Forcing the ferry to offload could trigger a crush on the pier; allowing departure risks capsizing. Another boat is not expected until morning. Alberto must decide what to do.
options: Allow the ferry to depart, with a lifejacket distribution and a slower speed requirement.
Order partial offloading of the heaviest cargo and the youngest passengers, risking tension at the dock.
Block departure entirely and keep the crowd calm with promises of a second boat at first light.
tension: risk to some vs. harm of crowd unrest

title: Who Gets the Last Spot on the Rescue Raft
scenario: Relief boat skipper Anders Mikkelsen, volunteering with a Danish sea rescue society, reaches a drifting fishing skiff in heavy swell with five people aboard, one of them a fellow volunteer, Sofie, who has gone out in bad weather to help and is now exhausted. His inflatable has room for four. The skiff's owner begs him to take his two sons first. Sofie says to take the others and leave her. Anders must decide who comes aboard and who waits for the second boat.
options: Take the two sons and two others, leaving Sofie with the owner, since she knowingly accepted the risk.
Take Sofie and the weakest passengers by medical need, whoever they are, regardless of the owner's plea.
Take four by drawing lots, treating every person on the skiff as equally deserving of a place.
